Something wild happened today that made me pause.

A client I've worked with for 10 years — deals over WhatsApp, handshake trust, same contract every time — suddenly comes back with a long list of objections. Objections they never had before.

Turns out? They ran our contract through AI.

So we ran their objections through AI. They replied with AI. Now we're in a closed loop. AI negotiating with AI. Humans watching from the sidelines.

Here's my question: Are we outsourcing trust?

The whole point of AI in contracts was to make the human's job easier — not to drag negotiations into endless back-and-forth. But I'm seeing this trend with multiple clients now. AI reviews. AI replies. AI objections.

We're losing the human-to-human negotiation that builds deals.

I believe AI should amplify us. Not complicate trust. Not replace the handshake. Not turn every deal into a legal chess match where neither side knows if they're talking to a person or a prompt.

This is Day 100 of building in public from Dubai. And this is the question we'll all face soon:

How do we keep the human at the center when AI is in the room?

Because if we lose the trust layer, we lose what makes deal-making human.

Your AI agent finished the task. Another AI graded it: PASS.

They can both be wrong.
So who checks the checker?
Generation got cheap.
Verification did not.

The old bottleneck was completing the task.
The new bottleneck is knowing whether the result is right.

Giving the model a confidence score is not verification.
Using a second model as a judge helps—but it does not make the judgment neutral.

A reliable evaluation system uses layers:
Deterministic checks for contracts, schemas, permissions and exact outcomes.

A calibrated LLM judge for fuzzy quality, guided by a written rubric and compared with expert labels.

Human judgment where context, ambiguity or consequences matter.

Production evidence to expose failures the original evaluation set missed.
This changes the role of QA.

QA is not the person manually checking every AI response.

QA becomes the person who:
defines what “correct” means;
identifies what must never break;
creates the golden data set;
chooses the right graders;
calibrates model judges against humans;
investigates failures and non-determinism;
sets release thresholds based on risk.

One distinction matters:
Evals measure behaviour.
Guardrails constrain live actions.
Humans own risk and escalation.
If an agent passes 96% of its evals, the critical issue is not the 96%.

It is whether the remaining 4% contains something you cannot afford to break.
Confidence is a claim. Evidence earns trust.

In the early days, a startup might have:
1 founder
2 developers
1 designer
1 person doing almost everything else.
And somehow, things work.

Then customers increase.
Features multiply.
Support requests grow.
New integrations are needed.
Suddenly, the same team that moved incredibly fast starts struggling to keep up.
This is where technology team scaling becomes critical.

The answer isn't always:
“Hire more developers.”

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁?

Here are 6 things startups should consider:
1️⃣ Hire for the next stage, not just today's workload
A developer who solves today's tickets may not be the person you need when the product reaches the next level.
Think about upcoming requirements: architecture, security, cloud, QA, DevOps, data, AI, and engineering leadership.

2️⃣ Build the core team carefully
Your first engineering hires have a huge impact.
They influence architecture, development practices, documentation, code quality, and eventually the culture of the entire technology organization.

3️⃣ Don't hire everything too early
Not every startup needs a large DevOps, QA, data, or security team from day one.
Build capabilities as the complexity and business requirements justify them.

4️⃣ Use flexible talent when appropriate
There are situations where hiring full-time employees isn't the only option.
Contract developers, specialists, staff augmentation, and external technology partners can help startups access skills without immediately building large permanent teams.

5️⃣ Invest in engineering processes
More developers don't automatically mean more productivity.
As the team grows, startups need better:

→ Documentation
→ Code reviews
→ Testing
→ Project management
→ CI/CD
→ Security practices
→ Communication
Without processes, growth can create chaos.

6️⃣ Keep technology aligned with business growth
Your technology team shouldn't operate separately from the business.
Engineering priorities should connect with customer needs, revenue goals, product strategy, and market opportunities.

🚨 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻:
Scaling a technology team isn't about reaching a specific headcount.
It's about building the right capabilities at the right time.

Too few people → delivery slows down.
Too many people too early → costs increase and coordination becomes harder.

The goal is balance.

Last week a founder asked me: "How do I know if my idea is even worth building?"

Real question. Most non-tech founders never get an honest answer to it — because everyone they talk to has something to sell them.

Agencies want a project. Freelancers want a contract. Nobody's incentive is to tell you "cut this feature" or "this isn't worth building yet."

So I built my process around answering that question honestly, first.

Before any code gets written, here's what I actually do:

→ Validate the idea against a real market gap, not just "sounds cool"
→ Cut the MVP down to the smallest thing that proves people want it
→ Recommend the right tech stack, with the reasoning behind it
→ Give a realistic cost + timeline — so no one can overquote you later
→ Hand over a one-page document any developer can build from

I've shipped 2 AI SaaS products solo (Crackit AI, ProdFlow AI) and written full technical blueprints for 6+ more — across fintech, travel, hiring, compliance. I've also audited other people's "AI" products and found features that were just regex pretending to be smart.

The founders who avoid that trap are the ones who get an honest opinion before they spend money — not after.

If you've got an idea and you're not sure it's worth building yet, drop it in the comments. I'll tell you straight.

 It's Firstsource Solutions, part of the RP-Sanjiv Goenka Group. They handle healthcare revenue cycle management, banking collections, mortgage servicing, and customer operations for clients in the US, UK, and Europe. The narrative around BPM companies has been grim — everyone assumed AI would take these jobs and shrink revenues. Firstsource flipped it: they're using AI to deliver better outcomes, win bigger deals, and grow margins. Q1 FY27 was their ninth consecutive quarter of double-digit revenue growth. EBIT margin has expanded seven quarters in a row. They're now recognized by Everest Group in RCM Intelligent Operations — clients are hiring them because of AI, not despite it.

When a Kenyan startup collapses, the employees on payroll might get a payout. The riders and gig workers who kept it running never had a contract to break.

Kenya's startups lost investors Sh93 billion this year, mostly from hiring fast to look big before running out of money. Someone on payroll can point to a contract, even if enforcing it takes a court case. A boda rider, a delivery courier, or a data annotator working through an app usually cannot. Kenya's gig economy moves KES 133 billion a year and involves roughly 1.5 million people who are, on paper, nobody's employee.

That gap is not an accident of paperwork. Kenya's Employment and Labour Relations Court ruled in June that a company cannot call a layoff "restructuring" without proving it happened. That protects people the law already recognises as employees. Most gig and platform workers in Kenya are still classified as independent contractors, so the same court has nothing to rule on when their income disappears overnight.

This is closer to who Kazi Pap's users actually are. Not the person with a contract to enforce. The rider, the courier, the data worker with none.

Parliament is reviewing a Labour Laws Amendment Bill that would classify some platform workers, delivery riders specifically, as employees or "dependent contractors" when they depend on one platform for most of their income. Glovo told the committee in June that this would undermine the flexibility gig work is built on. The bill is still under review.

I made a related argument in May, in a submission on Kenya's AI Bill. Its workforce impact clause assumes a formal employer to hold accountable. I argued that assumption fails 86 percent of Kenya's workforce and asked for the clause to name informal and platform workers directly. It has not been adopted yet.

Which matters more right now: getting platforms to call gig workers what they actually are, or getting AI policy to notice them at all?

2️⃣ Demand Forecasting
What people and skills will the business need in the future?

3️⃣ Supply Analysis
What talent and skills are currently available internally?

4️⃣ Gap Analysis
Identify headcount, skill and leadership gaps.

5️⃣ Workforce Actions
HR can respond through:
• Hiring
• Upskilling & reskilling
• Internal mobility
• Succession planning
• Contract/contingent workforce
• Automation & AI

6️⃣ Scenario Planning
Prepare workforce plans for expansion, slowdown, technology adoption or changing business requirements.

Buy: Hire external talent
Borrow: Use consultants, contractors or other flexible talent models

 Remember:

Manpower Planning → How many people do we need?
Workforce Planning → How many + what skills + when + where + cost?

This week, I focused on project architecture, clean packaging, data-layer separation, and practical debugging in a Spring Boot backend project.

The main focus was understanding how good project structure and debugging practices make backend development easier to maintain and troubleshoot.

 🔹 Standardized the project foundation around Spring Boot 3.4 and Java 17, along with a consistent Git branching and packaging structure.

 🔹 Structured the application into focused packages such as Controller, Service, Repository, Config, Constant, Util, Exception, and HTTP to keep responsibilities clearly separated.

 🔹 Practiced separating API request/response POJOs, database Entities, and internal microservice DTOs instead of reusing the same objects across different layers.

 🔹 Explored why keeping data objects separate across layers helps maintain clearer boundaries between API contracts, persistence models, and service communication.

 🔹 Designed payment status processing around a common interface, allowing different status processors to follow a consistent contract.

 🔹 Applied the Factory Pattern to dynamically select the required payment status processor based on the payment status.

 🔹 Connected the package structure with the payment-processing design, keeping status-processing responsibilities organized rather than mixing them across unrelated classes.

 🔹 Practiced debugging the application using IDE breakpoints to pause execution at specific points and inspect the actual runtime flow.

 🔹 Used Step Over, Step Into, and Resume to trace execution through different parts of the backend and understand how the code behaves during runtime.

 🔹 Inspected runtime variable values while debugging, building a more practical understanding of how to identify and troubleshoot issues instead of relying only on code inspection.

India's IT job market is having an identity crisis right now.

On one side: Oracle, PayPal, Amazon, Adidas and Meta have together cut 12,000–15,000 roles in India in the past 12 months. TCS and other majors have trimmed headcount too. Globally, ~130,000 layoffs so far in 2026 alone (layoffs.fyi).

On the other side: GCCs are projected to add 120,000 specialized roles this year. Semicon 2.0 + PLI could create 200,000+ direct and indirect jobs by 2030. Festive-season gig hiring alone could add 2-2.5 lakh jobs.

Same economy, opposite headlines. Here's the actual pattern:

→ Routine coding, testing, back-office work, shrinking
→ AI, cybersecurity, product design, advanced analytics, growing
→ Legacy engineering headcount, out
→ Niche, specialized, outcome-driven roles, in

And it's not just anecdotal anymore, reports suggest Big Tech's shift toward AI-driven delivery could put up to $20B of traditional IT outsourcing revenue at risk, as clients renegotiate contracts around automation instead of headcount.

The takeaway for anyone starting their career right now (me included): "IT job" isn't one category anymore. There's a shrinking half and a growing half, and which one you're in matters a lot more than the fact that you're "in tech" at all.

What side of this are you positioning yourself on?

What if I don't Get Employment
                   Dr. Ratnakar Gedam
                          Dt. 23.09.2026

Unemployment is forced upon an educated person by the govt system.

Before 2014, there were certain institutional arrangements such as Employment Exchange, Recruitment Boards, etc. Gradually all have eroded, became defunct and closed. 

Parents often suggest why don't you either find work in the private/ corporate sector or start your own small businesses. 

LL. B. and LL. M. Degree holders were appearing for Bar Council Registration Exams, State Judiciary Exams and working in law firms, working as junior to senior lawyer etc. 

Recent time has witnessed the advent of AI Tools which are unavoidable or inevitable in days to come. AI Tools for Lawyer & legal area have expanded scope of employability. Those who knows AI and those who do not know AI.

Paralegal Work is growing both domestically and in advanced countries like the US, EU, Canara, Australia etc.

Assumptions & presumption often create confusions in choice of work. The presumption that the US, EU etc  have huge work and out of 193 countries only Indias will be given job, or assumption that advanced countries are benevolent to Indians or assumption that Indian firms don't need paralegal work for contracting out to outside their firm employees etc. The trade-off option solve such dilemma. All educated youths or lawyers do not have acumen for business. Job is best as it eliminates all uncertainties of losses and getting continuous flow of orders & work etc. 

Start-ups are in need of external help. About 200 paralegal activities related to corporate exist in India and in the US, EU, UK, Canada, Australia etc. Law graduate should explore those area. Work involves legal understanding and use of computers to fill up the columns, to get registation, aproval, Authorization etc. and use of AI tools when needed for legal research or corporate research.

Paralegal Work can be broadly categorised as:
1. Formation of company & Founder Agreements & Contractor
2. Recruitment/hiring of Employees & HR job contract drafting
3. Drafting Contracts related to Intellectual Property, Trad Mark, Doing Business As, etc.
4. Drafting of Privacy Policy, Confidential, Data Collection & Data Protection, Information Policy etc.
5. Customs & Sales, Domestic & International Sales
6. Technological Use, Start-Ups Contracts
7. Vendor & Procurement Contract Drafting
8. Marketing & Advertisement
9. Financing & Investors Contract
10. Banking, Finance & Security
11. Dispute Resolution mechanism 

Similarly, Beside knowledge of use of Computer System, Legal Background aspirants of paralegal work should know use of AI Tools.

Usually, all study but opportunities to draft Anticipatory Bail, SLP, Temporary Injunction, Divorce by Mutual Consent, Contract Negotiations, etc. isn't available. AI tool are capable of handling these activities.

The GCC 5.0 Advisory Matrix: Who Is Running Your Global Expansion Playbook?

India’s GCC advisory market has hit an inflection point. Driven by an unprecedented surge, GCCs adding 200K employees in FY26, double the hiring rate of traditional ITOs - nasscom. The global C-suite faces an absolute maze of consulting partners.

When a Fortune 500 decides to build an AI product factory or an IP fortress in India, they no longer default automatically to legacy buying choices.

The advisory market has fragmented into four distinct archetypes: MBBs, Big 4s, Boutiques, and the New Wave of BPOs/ITOs. Understanding where each player excels is critical for any global executive designing their India footprint.

Strategy-Led MBBs like McKinsey India Boston Consulting Group (BCG) operate at the absolute peak of boardroom hierarchy. They own macro-level mandates, answering complex global portfolio questions - should an enterprise scale engineering ecosystem in India? what does the long-term strategic ROI looks like? Offering top-down, relationship-driven engagement models focused on Corp Strategy/ M&A at premium, fixed priced fees, with deal sizes spanning $1M to $5M+.

The #Big4 like EY , PwC India , Deloitte , KPMG India serve as primary engine for cross-border ops compliance, enterprise risk mitigation, answering structural questions around global corporate data framework, India’s strict DPDP Act, tax and transfer pricing. Their go-to-market strategy relies heavily on multi-tier cross-selling with typical deal sizes of $500K to $2M+.

Boutiques, such as Zinnov or ANSR , have built a distinct competitive advantage by operating as high-velocity execution partners. They answer specific, tactical problems - where to source 50 specialized LLM security engineers? how to structure their product pods? Boutiques win through a high-touch, research-driven GTM model built on deep, localized market intelligence. They offer end-to-end "GCC-as-a-Service" models, complete talent mapping, and local ecosystem integration with lean deal sizes averaging $150K to $600K.

The New Wave (BPO/ ITOs) dominate when an enterprise prioritizes large-scale operational transition over core product design. Their mandates focus on rapid deployment, answering operational scale questions like how to quickly lift and shift global IT infrastructure and service desk operations to an asset-light delivery center. They build bottom-up relationships by offering deep volume discounting on technical infrastructure provisioning. They utilize transactional, cost-per-FTE managed services pricing, leading to large, multi-year contracts valued between $2M and $10M+.

Scaling your next global innovation engine? are you paying for a high-level strategic deck, or are you partnering for speed and precise local execution?

GCC hiring is changing — and it’s not just about hiring more people.

One shift that’s becoming increasingly visible in India’s GCC ecosystem is the growing use of flexible and contractual talent.

According to recent industry data, contractual roles now account for roughly 25% of GCC hiring/workforce, compared with around 18% two years ago.

Why the shift?

→ Faster access to specialised talent
→ Project-based demand and shorter transformation timelines
→ Growing need for niche skills in AI, data, cloud and cybersecurity
→ The ability to scale teams without immediately committing to permanent headcount
→ Greater adoption of contract-to-hire models

But there’s an important nuance here:

This isn’t permanent hiring versus contract hiring.

It’s increasingly becoming permanent + flexible + contract-to-hire, depending on the capability, project and business need.

And as GCCs continue moving from delivery centres towards higher-value technology, product and transformation functions, the workforce model will have to evolve with them.

The interesting question is no longer just:

“How many people are GCCs hiring?”

It’s increasingly:

“What kind of talent do they need, how quickly do they need it, and what’s the right workforce model to get there?”

That, to me, is where the next phase of GCC hiring gets interesting. 🚀

Agentic Commerce Is Coming to Procurement. Are We Ready?
 
I once cheered a 5% cut in procurement cycle time.
Now AI agents are promising to remove entire manual steps.
The Indian Express covered Amazon Pay’s Smart Wallet and NPCI’s MyUPI at Global Fintech Fest. It made me think about what comes next for procurement: agentic commerce, where agents can search, compare and, within set limits, act on a buyer’s behalf.
Gartner predicts that AI agents will sit in the middle of 90% of B2B buying by 2028. That does not mean every purchase will be autonomous. But it raises a real question: what should we delegate?
I almost stayed quiet. I have used AI for demand forecasting. I have not yet used an AI agent to buy, and I am still moving from uniform to corporate life.
But the questions that matter are a buyer’s questions. So, I am looking at this through three of them:
Why does it matter?
Procurement means spending money entrusted to us. Every purchase carries accountability.
How should it work?
Agents can misread instructions or go beyond their limits. So, we need clear limits, a named person who remains accountable and an independent check. Who authorises the purchase? Who reviews exceptions? Who can stop the agent?
What changes?
An agent does not just advise. It acts. That makes the quality of our data and controls even more important.
My starting point would be low risk repeat orders from approved catalogues, bid comparisons and order tracking, where requirements are clear and exceptions can be escalated.
The people question matters too. In a Gartner survey, 55% of supply chain leaders expected agentic AI to reduce entry level hiring needs. That leaves me wondering: if agents do the routine work, how will new buyers develop the judgement to supervise them?
Here is how I would prepare:
•      Assess spend by business risk as well as how routine it is.
•      Clean item, supplier and price data in the ERP.
•      Pilot a small set of low risk purchases under existing contracts.
•      Set value caps, approved suppliers, approval rules, escalation points and a way to stop the agent.
•      Record the agent’s actions and retain purchase order, receipt and invoice checks.
•      Train the team to supervise agents, while giving new buyers chances to build judgement.
Automate the routine. Guard the critical.
How do you see agentic commerce changing procurement? Share your view.

Six weeks into a project this year, a client asked me: "Can you just build us an AI team instead?"

Their board had approved budget for it. On paper, saying yes was the easy win — bigger contract, more visibility, "we built their AI team" as a case study.

It also went against everything Feneco stands for.

Teams don't fix a lack of automation. They fix a lack of clarity about what actually needs automating. Most companies I meet don't need more people thinking about AI — they need 3-4 of their existing processes automated properly and wired into the tools they already use.

So I said no to the team, and asked a different question instead: which parts of your operation are slow because of missing automation, not missing headcount?

We spent the next two weeks mapping their approval workflows instead of writing job descriptions. What looked like a staffing gap turned out to be a handful of specific bottlenecks, none of which needed a new hire.

The lesson stuck with me: the pressure to "build an AI capability" is often really a request for permission to avoid prioritizing. Hiring feels like progress. Automating a few things well feels smaller ... until it's the thing that actually moves the business.

If you're facing a similar decision right now "team vs. targeted automation" I'd genuinely like to hear which way you're leaning, and why.

At Feneco, we believe the fastest way to slow an AI initiative down is to hire for it before you've prioritized it.

Apple killed its server business in 2011 and told the enterprise market to go buy someone else's rack. The AI boom just changed its mind.

The Information reported this week that Apple is developing an enterprise server built on its own chips, potentially pairing them with Nvidia networking technology, aimed at AI developers, businesses, and governments. The plan reportedly includes two versions, the smaller one built around two of Apple's next-generation M8 chips. Apple has spent fifteen years positioning itself as a consumer and creative-professional hardware company that happens to sell some machines to developers. A dedicated AI enterprise server aimed at governments and AI labs is a different business, with different customers, different support contracts, and a sales motion Apple hasn't run at scale since Xserve.

The timing tells you what actually changed. Apple has decided the silicon inside an AI server is worth owning too, enough to reenter a business it spent over a decade avoiding.

I've watched companies re-enter markets they'd previously walked away from the moment the economics flipped, and the tell is always the same: nobody says "we changed our mind," they just quietly start hiring for the org chart the old business used to have.

Pairing your own chips with Nvidia's networking is a tell of its own. Apple is betting on a narrower thing: a profitable seat at the table for whoever controls the compute, even if someone else controls the plumbing between racks.
